verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna is at the edge of his strength. They have laid down their bow and told Krishna that the mind is too restless, too powerful to hold. It feels like trying to catch the wind. Krishna does not argue. They agree that the mind is stubborn and hard to control. But Krishna says that through practice and by letting go, the mind can be trained. It is not a promise that the storm will stop, but that you can learn to stand in it without being swept away.
verse.for_you: The phone is the wind you are trying to catch. Today, notice when the mind pulls you toward the screen. Just name it, and let go. One quiet minute of rest is enough to begin.

verse.speaker: Rama
verse.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse.sanskrit: चेतः पतति कार्येषु विहगः स्वामिषेष्विव । क्षणेन विरतिं याति बालः क्रीडनकादिव ॥
verse.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.
verse.why: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

prasang.title: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.story_hook: In front of the whole court, the young prince stood up and said what everyone feels and nobody says.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

verse.meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vasishtha and Vishvamitra. He has been trying to rule and has seen how hollow it all feels. He tells them his mind behaves like a bird. It swoops onto a task for a quick bite, then flies off without a thought. A moment later it is gone, leaving the task behind like a bored child tossing aside a toy. This is the truth of a mind left to its own devices. It does not stay long enough to finish anything, and it never fills.
verse.for_you: Your phone does the same thing. It offers a quick bite of a video and then drops it. Notice that empty feeling when you close the app. That emptiness is the bird, not the exam. Name it as emptiness before you open the next screen.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.sanskrit: यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः । इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
verse.line: Like a tortoise pulling in its limbs, draw your senses back from what pulls at them.
verse.translation: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side, a person withdraws the senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly set.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna. He asks what a steady person looks like. Krishna says a steady person is like a tortoise. When the world gets loud, the tortoise pulls its limbs inside. It keeps its body safe. In the same way, when you draw your senses back from what pulls at them, your wisdom holds. Steadiness is not about doing more. It is about letting go of the pull. That quiet pull-back is where your mind begins to rest.
verse.for_you: Today, when the phone calls for your attention, try pulling one sense back. Close one app and leave the room. That one quiet minute is your tortoise shell. It is enough to begin.

verse.speaker: Yama
verse.sanskrit: यस्त्वविज्ञानवान्भवत्ययुक्तेन मनसा सदा । तस्येन्द्रियाण्यवश्यानि दुष्टाश्वा इव सारथेः ॥ यस्तु विज्ञानवान्भवति युक्तेन मनसा सदा । तस्येन्द्रियाणि वश्यानि सदश्वा इव सारथेः ॥
verse.line: Without understanding, the senses bolt like wild horses; with a steady mind, they run like trained ones.
verse.translation: For one who lacks understanding, whose mind is never held steady, the senses run out of control like a driver's wild horses. For one who has understanding, whose mind is always steady, the senses obey like good horses.
verse.why: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.

prasang.title: The chariot of the self
prasang.summary: Yama pictures a person as a chariot: the self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the driver, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. With a steady mind the horses obey; without it they bolt. He ends with the call to arise and wake.
prasang.lesson: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.

verse.meaning: Yama is still speaking to Nachiketa about the chariot that carries the self. He says the senses are the horses. When a person has no understanding of what is real, the senses run wild like horses with no reins. They bolt in every direction, driven by desire. But when the mind is steady and clear, those same senses obey like trained horses, running exactly where the rider wants. The mind is the reins. Without it, the body and senses drive the person. Without it, there is no stopping the chase.
verse.for_you: Your phone is a horse that runs where it wants to run. You can hold the reins. When you pick up your phone, notice the pull. Then let your hand rest. This is the steady mind. This is the driver.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse.sanskrit: यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम् । ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
verse.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
verse.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.
verse.why: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

prasang.title: Meditation in detail
prasang.summary: Krishna describes meditation: moderation in food and sleep, the mind like a lamp in a windless place, bringing the wandering mind back, and feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
prasang.lesson: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

verse.meaning: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to meditate. He says the mind is restless and unsteady. It will wander. The instruction is not to fight it or force it. Wherever it goes, one should gently draw it back. This must be done again and again. The practice is one of moderation and gentle return. The mind is trained not by breaking it, but by bringing it back, over and over.
verse.for_you: Today, when your mind drifts to the screen, do not scold yourself. Just notice. Then gently bring your attention back to your breath. Do this one time, and then again if it happens. That is the practice.

prasang.title: Prahlada: effort and grace are not rivals
prasang.summary: After telling how Prahlada awakened, Vasishtha faces Rama's challenge: if everything comes by effort, wasn't Prahlada saved by Vishnu's grace? Vasishtha answers that Prahlada earned it himself, that the Self and Vishnu are not two, and that sometimes we wake by our own effort and sometimes by grace reached through devotion. Steady daily practice ripens the mind like a mango.
prasang.lesson: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha is speaking to Rama, after the story of Prahlada. He says that through daily practice and discernment the mind soon becomes clear, just as a mango slowly ripens into its sweetness. This means that grace and effort work together, and that steady daily practice ripens the mind like a mango.
verse.for_you: You do not need to clear your mind today. You only need to sit with it for one minute, away from the phone. Let the mind be as it is, like an unripe mango. Keep showing up tomorrow, and let it ripen slowly.

story.title: Hanuman meets Surasa on the way
story.story_hook: Halfway across the ocean, something opened its mouth in front of him.
story.summary: Leaping the ocean, Hanuman refuses to rest on a friendly mountain until the work is done. Surasa blocks him and opens her jaws; he doubles his size each time she widens them, then shrinks tiny and slips in and out. A demon that catches flyers by grabbing their shadows tries the same trick, and he sees through it at once.
story.lesson: Meet obstacles with flexibility: sometimes bigger, sometimes smaller, never stuck.

script: Your mind will not settle. You are trying to focus on your studies, but your attention keeps slipping away. The phone is in your hand, and the stress is building. You feel scattered, and you do not know how to make it stop.

Arjuna has just told Krishna that he cannot control his own mind. He says it is like trying to catch the wind. The wind is everywhere, and it cannot be held. Krishna listens to this. He does not argue. He agrees that the mind is stubborn. And then he says:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम्, तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम्.
In plain words: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.

This is a hard truth to live with. The mind is not supposed to be perfectly quiet. It wants to move, to wander, to chase the next thing. That is what makes it feel so stormy. But Krishna does not say to fight the wind. He says to train it with practice. And that means letting go. You do not need to stop every thought. You only need to notice when it has pulled you away.
The phone is the wind you are trying to catch. Today, notice when your mind pulls you toward the screen. Just name it. And then let go. One quiet minute of rest is enough to begin.
Can you give your mind one quiet minute today?

depth.life: Your mind pulls you toward the phone, and the screen feeds the restlessness. You feel scattered, and the hours slip by without focus. The stress is vague because the real trouble is this constant pull.
depth.points: The mind is naturally restless, like the wind. It is not your fault, but it is your task to train it. Practice and letting go are the only ways to calm it.
depth.practice: Sit for one quiet minute before touching the phone in the morning.
depth.question: What does the mind want when it pulls you to the screen?
